q.intro.text: A pair of sneakers cost forty dollars. Now the same pair costs fifty dollars. By what percent did the price go up? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Let's work it out in four steps. Press each step, and watch the picture first.

e.step0.text: The price before the change, forty dollars, is the base. It is one hundred percent. Cut it into four equal parts: each part is ten dollars, or twenty-five percent.

e.step1.text: The price went up by ten dollars. That's the change. It is not the new price.

e.step2.text: The ten dollars is exactly one of the four parts of the base. Ten out of forty is one fourth, and one fourth is twenty-five percent.

e.step3.text: So the price went up twenty-five percent: a twenty-five percent increase. Fifty dollars is one hundred twenty-five percent of forty dollars, but the change is twenty-five percent.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why divide by forty, and not by fifty?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. The base is the amount before the change. Here, that's forty dollars.

e.why.big.text: No. Here the base, forty dollars, is the smaller number. The base is the amount before the change, whether it is bigger or smaller.

e.why.diff.text: Ten dollars is the change in dollars. A percent compares it with the base: ten out of forty is twenty-five percent.

t.intro.text: Now a phone's price drops from two hundred fifty dollars to two hundred dollars. I'll do the first two steps. Then it's your turn.

t.pct.text: What percent of the base is the fifty dollar change?

t.pct.ok.text: Yes. Fifty dollars is one of the five equal parts of two hundred fifty. One fifth is twenty percent.

t.pct.base.text: That compares fifty with two hundred, the new price. The base is the price before the change: two hundred fifty dollars.

t.pct.diff.text: Fifty is the change in dollars. Compare it with the base: fifty out of two hundred fifty.

t.pct.left.text: Eighty percent is what's left. Two hundred dollars is eighty percent of two hundred fifty. The change is the part that came off.

t.pct.other.text: Not quite. Count the parts: the base is cut into five equal parts, and the change is one of them.

t.name.ok.text: Yes. A twenty percent decrease. The price went down by one fifth of what it was.

t.name.dir.text: The size is right, but the price went down. That's a decrease.

t.name.left.text: Two hundred dollars is eighty percent of the old price. The price went down by the other part: twenty percent.

t.name.base.text: Twenty-five percent compares fifty with the new price. Use the price before the change: twenty percent.

t.back.right.text: At the start you picked twenty-five percent. You were right, and now you can show why: the ten dollar change is one fourth of the forty dollar base.

t.back.new.text: At the start you picked twenty percent. That divides ten by fifty, the new price. The base is the price before: forty dollars. So it's twenty-five percent.

t.back.diff.text: At the start you picked ten percent. Ten dollars is the change in dollars. Compared with the forty dollar base, it's twenty-five percent.

t.back.none.text: At the start: forty dollars to fifty dollars is a twenty-five percent increase.

t.sure1.text: You said you were pretty sure.

t.done.text: Same rule both times: the change is compared with the amount before the change.

p.intro.text: The sneakers went from forty dollars to fifty dollars: a twenty-five percent increase. Then they go on sale, back to forty dollars. Sam says: that's a twenty-five percent decrease. Is Sam right?

p.build.wrong.text: Then prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build.right.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Right. Fifty minus forty is ten. The sale takes ten dollars off.

p.c2.text: This time the base is fifty dollars, the price before the sale. Cut it into five equal parts of ten dollars.

p.c3.text: Ten dollars is one of those five parts: one fifth, or twenty percent. So it's a twenty percent decrease, not twenty-five.

p.done.text: That's a proof. The same ten dollars, but a different base: up twenty-five percent, then down only twenty percent.

p.no.cancel.text: That's Sam's idea, the one we're testing. Going up and coming down don't use the same base.

p.no.big.text: Here fifty dollars is the base, but not because it is bigger. It's the price before the sale. In the rise from forty to fifty, the base was the smaller forty.

p.no.diff.text: Ten dollars is the change in dollars, not a percent. A percent compares it with the base.

p.no.other.text: True, but it's the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?
